teaser: A marsh painted without a single drop of water, and a poem hidden in five syllables.
review_notes:
The image shows only ONE screen of the Met's pair of six-panel screens (apparently the right-hand one, with signature and seal at its right edge); the lesson says so.
Date: the Met dates the pair 'after 1709'; 1710 is an approximation.
Dimensions: each screen about 163.7 x 352.4 cm.
Pigments: blue from azurite and green from malachite are the standard mineral pigments for such screens; assumed here rather than taken from a technical report.
Korin's family business Kariganeya (luxury textiles for court ladies) and his squandered inheritance: standard biography.
Earlier 'Irises' screens (Nezu Museum, Tokyo, c. 1701-05) without the bridge: standard.
Acquired by the Met in 1953: per museum credit line.
The acrostic poem (ka-ki-tsu-ba-ta) from Tales of Ise, episode 9: paraphrased, not quoted.

lesson.text: Zero. That is how much water Ogata Kōrin painted in this picture of a swamp. Irises of this kind grow with their feet in the wet, and the wooden walkway exists only to keep travelers dry. Yet there is no ripple, no reflection, no bank. Just gold.

He left out more than that. No sky, no ground, no people. The image you see is one folding screen of a pair, about 3.5 meters wide (11 and a half feet), and it holds exactly two things: flowers and planks. For Kōrin's first viewers, those two things were enough to tell a whole story.

The story comes from the Tales of Ise, a book of poems and short episodes written some eight hundred years before Kōrin. A courtier, out of favor in the capital, travels east with friends. They stop to eat at a place called Yatsuhashi, “Eight Bridges”, where a river splits into eight channels, each crossed by a plank bridge. Irises are in bloom.

Someone dares the courtier to write a poem in which each of the five lines starts with one syllable of the flower's name: ka, ki, tsu, ba, ta. He does, and the poem is about the wife he left behind. His friends cry so hard that their tears soak the dried rice they are eating.
Kōrin paints a story by removing the storyteller. Flowers plus a plank bridge was a code: any educated viewer supplied the traveler, the poem and the homesickness.

With the characters gone, the picture has to hold itself up by design alone. And Kōrin was raised on design. His family ran Kariganeya, a Kyoto shop that made luxurious kimono fabrics for the ladies of the court. He grew up among pattern books, and it shows in how he lays shapes across a surface.
Trace how the screen is organized. It is closer to a textile pattern than to a view.

lines.label: The zigzag
lines.text: The bridge climbs from the left edge to the top in a stepped line: flat, slanted, flat, slanted. It is seen from straight above, like a diagram, while the flowers are seen from the side.

lines.label: The rising bloom
lines.text: The blue flower heads drift upward from lower left to upper right, crossing under the bridge. Two diagonals travel together, like a melody and its bass line.

lines.label: The quiet corner
lines.text: The lower right is left almost bare. That empty gold is where the water would be. Kōrin tucks his signature into it.

lesson.text: Two viewpoints in one image, then: a bridge in plan, flowers in profile. It breaks every rule of realistic space and nobody minds, because nothing here pretends to be a window. The gold leaf, laid in small squares, is a flat wall. The pigments are worth a closer view.

lesson.title: Three materials
lesson.text: Blue, green and gray. Each is handled in a different way.

spots.title: Ground stone
spots.text: The petals are a thick mineral blue, traditionally made from crushed azurite. Darker and lighter blues sit side by side with no shading between them, so each flower reads as a cut-out shape.

spots.title: Blades
spots.text: The leaves are single strokes of opaque green, one per blade, with no veins and no outlines. Where they overlap they simply merge into a green mass.

spots.title: Weathered wood
spots.text: The planks are ink, not mineral color. Kōrin let wet ink puddle and dry in blotches, a technique named tarashikomi. The stains become moss and rain-soaked timber.

lesson.text: So the most expensive materials, gold and ground stone, are applied flat and clean, and the humblest one, ink, is allowed to run wild. The bridge is the only thing on the screen that looks old and touched by weather. It is also the only thing people built.

Kōrin spent his inheritance fast, on parties and fine things, and was nearly forty and short of money when he turned to painting for a living. The title “Hokkyō” that he writes before his name here was an honorary rank granted to artists, which he received in 1701.
The planks do not float. They rest on posts driven into the mud, tied in pairs with crossbars, and Kōrin shows these supports sticking out from under the walkway in several places.
Most posts hide under the bridge. Find the spot where a row of post tops pokes up above a plank.

spots.title: Post tops
spots.text: Four short stubs with greenish caps rise above the top plank. Below the bridge, the same posts appear as little grids of crossed timber. They are the only hint that there is depth under the gold.

lesson.text: This was not his first try at the subject. Around ten years earlier he had painted a pair of screens with irises alone, no bridge at all, now in the Nezu Museum in Tokyo. Coming back to it, he added the planks, and with them the journey.
The screens crossed an ocean much wider than the courtier's road east. The Metropolitan Museum of Art bought the pair in 1953, and it is one of the best-known Japanese paintings outside Japan.

quiz.question: What did the courtier's poem at Yatsuhashi have to do?
options: Begin each line with a syllable of the iris's name
quiz.explanation: Each of its five lines starts with ka, ki, tsu, ba or ta.

quiz.question: From which angle is the bridge shown?
options: From the side, like the flowers
quiz.explanation: The bridge is seen from straight above while the irises are in profile.

quiz.question: Which part of the screen is painted with pooled, blotchy ink?
quiz.explanation: Kōrin used tarashikomi on the planks to suggest weathered wood.

quiz.question: What was the business of Kōrin's family?
quiz.explanation: The family shop, Kariganeya, supplied fine textiles to court ladies.

quiz.question: How does this work differ from Kōrin's earlier iris screens in Tokyo?
quiz.explanation: The earlier pair shows irises alone; here the planks bring in the journey.

facts.text: Kōrin painted the water of the marsh in silver.
facts.explanation: There is no water at all: the gold ground stands in for it.

facts.text: No person appears anywhere on the screen.
facts.explanation: The traveler of the story is left out; flowers and bridge are enough to evoke him.

facts.text: Kōrin became a professional painter as a teenager.
facts.explanation: He turned to painting for a living when he was nearly forty, after spending his inheritance.
